analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to manufacture, sell, or import semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines over 15 rounds.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 30, 2025 with 193 House Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the same day and has had no hearing, markup, or floor vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to knowingly import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons — defined by features like pistol grips, threaded barrels, and detachable magazines, plus a long list of named models — and magazines holding more than 15 rounds. Guns people already legally own would be 'grandfathered': they could keep them, and could even sell them to someone who passes a background check. Hunting-style, bolt-action, lever-action, and rimfire firearms are exempt. The bill also requires secure storage of grandfathered weapons, serial numbers and date stamps on new devices, and lets states use existing federal grant money to pay people who turn in covered guns through buy-back programs.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities affected by mass shootings, who would face a smaller supply of the semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines most often used in high-casualty attacks. Current owners of covered guns keep theirs under the grandfather clause, and police, retired officers, and nuclear-material security personnel are exempt.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines holding more than 15 rounds.
Grandfathers guns lawfully owned before enactment: owners may keep them, and a licensed dealer must run a background check before a private sale or transfer of a grandfathered weapon.
Spares hunting and sporting firearms: manually operated bolt, pump, and lever guns, rimfire rifles, antiques, and hundreds of named hunting rifles and shotguns are exempt from the ban.

Requires grandfathered assault weapons to be securely stored away from people legally barred from owning guns, requires serial numbers and manufacture dates on new weapons and magazines, and lets states use Edward Byrne Memorial grant funds to pay individuals who surrender covered guns in buy-back programs.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and importers lose the legal market for the covered rifles, pistols, and shotguns and for magazines over 15 rounds — a large share of the modern sporting-rifle business. Owners of covered guns face new storage requirements and background-checked transfers, and federal grant dollars would go to buy-back payments.

drawbacks.text: The ban is defined by features rather than function, so it sweeps in rifles and shotguns with pistol grips, threaded barrels, or adjustable stocks that critics call ordinary hunting and sporting guns, and the exemptions cover only weapons lawfully owned before the bill takes effect.

The grandfather clause means every covered gun already in circulation stays legal to keep — and for weapons, to sell with a background check — so the ban affects the future supply, not the existing stock.

The bill's own stated purpose is 'to ensure that the right to keep and bear arms is not unlimited,' acknowledging it takes a contested position on the Second Amendment that opponents challenge in court; a ban this broad would face immediate litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the firearms most often used in high-casualty shootings while leaving hunting rifles, shotguns, and every lawfully owned gun in place, which softens the burden on owners. The real costs fall on manufacturers' future sales and on a contested Second Amendment question that courts would have to settle. The main design weakness is that grandfathering preserves the existing stock of covered weapons for decades.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever since.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucy McBath (D-GA) introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2025 on April 30, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
193 of the House's 217 Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans appear among the cosponsors.
The committee has taken no further action on the bill, and no floor vote has occurred, since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, firearms manufacturers and opponents of the ban are better off: with no committee action and a House majority that has not scheduled it, the bill has not advanced at all, while its supporters' nearly 200 cosponsors have produced nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and ban opponents, so far

for.name: Rep. Lucy McBath
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 193 Democratic cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Chairs the committee where the bill was referred; the committee has held no hearing or markup on it.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: 223 of 440 voting House members; controls the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill and the majority has not brought it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor listed is a Democrat — 193 of 217 House Democrats — and no Republican has signed on, so the bill's support is entirely one-sided.

industries.note: The bill criminalizes manufacturing the covered rifles, pistols, shotguns, and magazines over 15 rounds — a core product line for makers of AR-15-style and similar firearms. The industry's interest in blocking the bill runs against the public-safety case its supporters make for it.

Selling or transferring covered weapons would become a federal crime except for grandfathered guns moved through a licensed dealer with a background check, shrinking the legal dealer market for these firearms.
Importing covered weapons or large-capacity magazines would become a federal crime, cutting off imported models like AK-pattern and Saiga firearms listed in the bill.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a 223-seat House majority, no Republican support, and no committee action six months after referral, the bill is almost certain to die in committee without a vote, as previous assault weapons ban proposals have in divided Congresses.
